_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt: Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Cariboo Voices & Local News' — stories FROM and ABOUT the Cariboo-Chilcotin region and its communities. Score 80-100 for articles directly covering: news and events in Williams Lake, Quesnel, 100 Mile House, Bella Coola, Horsefly, Likely, Anahim Lake, Alexis Creek, or the Cariboo Regional District; local government and civic decisions (City of Williams Lake, City of Quesnel, CRD, District of 100 Mile House); local health services and emergency closures; local economy, businesses, and community programs; Cariboo arts, culture, and community events; AND digital equity, rural internet access (fiber, fixed wireless, Starlink), and connectivity serving these specific communities. Articles from local Cariboo news sources (mycariboonow.com, wltribune.com, quesnelobserver.com, 100milefreepress.net, cfjctoday.com) covering Cariboo community life should score 65-85. Score 50-79 for: BC provincial news directly affecting Cariboo communities, rural Canadian community stories closely paralleling Cariboo life, digital equity and rural internet broadly. Score 20-49 for: general BC news that may affect rural areas, broader rural Canada topics without specific Cariboo tie-in. Score 0-19 for: national/international news without Cariboo relevance, pure tech or entertainment with no community angle. Penalise heavily (score 0–20): international geopolitical and war news with no Cariboo tie-in; science discoveries without a local community connection; consumer tech reviews and gadget guides; wildlife and conservation stories not involving Cariboo communities or First Nations; BC provincial news without direct Cariboo-region relevance. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [scitechdaily.com] Studies link supportive childhoods and father involvement to well-being
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A study led by the University of Nottingham found that adults in the United Kingdom, United States and Japan who recalled more supportive childhood experiences reported better health, greater happiness and life satisfaction and lower anxiety [scitechdaily.com#1]. More supportive childhood experiences were also associated with stronger social connections, a greater sense of neighborhood belonging and more trust in others. The study, published Sept. 30 in the Journal of Happiness Studies, surveyed adults ages 18 to 34 [scitechdaily.com#1]. The findings show associations, not proof that childhood experiences caused adult outcomes: participants recalled their upbringing and reported their current well-being [scitechdaily.com#1]. Separately, a review of fatherhood research described links between sustained positive father involvement and children’s cognitive, social and emotional outcomes, while noting that the findings were correlational [time.com#1].

items.title: [Fast Company] What to think about before making a big ask from your direct reports
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

As a supervisor, you have some ability to dictate what your direct reports work on. The requests you make should typically fit their job description, though most descriptions have a catchall “other duties as assigned” attached, which is likely to cover you.

That said, the jobs you give someone generally have a particular expectation of the skills required, the hours to be worked, and the stress level associated with the tasks. If you’re going to ask someone to do something that far exceeds the norm, there are a few things you should consider first.

Are you taking advantage?

The people you supervise probably want to keep you happy. You have power over their evaluations, and your recommendation can help to propel them to a promotion or other opportunities. This means that when you ask your reports to do something, they are likely to agree.

You should make sure that when you’re making a big ask, the employee is likely to benefit rather than suffer from doing the work. For example, you have work that needs to be done, but you don’t want to put the time of a higher-priced employee onto it. If you’re going to try to save money by using a less-experienced person, you should be careful that you’re not adding a lot of extra hours or stress to their work just to cut costs.

Your reports pay attention to the hours that other people are putting in. If you ask far greater effort of them than you put in yourself, that can rankle in ways that may ultimately cause dedicated people to want to work elsewhere.

What are the long-term benefits?

When you are going to make that big ask, think about what benefits that work is likely to have for your direct report. Talk to them about those benefits when you make the request.

For example, a big project may give a newer employee a chance to work with senior leaders, or do work that is visible to them. That can help bring them future opportunities. A significant project may also help them to expand their capacities by taking on new experiences. That project may also lead to overtime (depending on how they are paid), allowing them to take home more money.

One reason for thinking through the benefits of this additional work for an employee is that you may discover that the assignment might be more beneficial for another member of your team. The more you can use significant tasks to develop your team, the easier it is to ask them to go beyond the norm.

What will sweeten the deal?

Of course, there are also some pretty onerous tasks that someone has to take on—and you may decide that burden should fall on one of your team members. In this situation, consider whether there are ways to make the burden less significant.

If the job is going to require additional travel or a lot of extra hours, you might want to offer compensatory time off or some time with a flexible work arrangement to reward them for taking one for the team.

If you’re going to give a team member a significant responsibility that adds effort and stress to their work, consider ways to help use that to further their career. Give that person additional mentorship to accelerate their career path or provide them with chances to engage with senior leaders who might ultimately be able to find additional opportunities for them.

When you use big asks as a way to give flexibility or career benefit to your team members, you create trust. The members of your team will talk to each other, and you don’t want to get the reputation of someone who drives people hard without looking out for them. When you give people challenge as well as support, you provide a motivating environment that allows the team to excel, even under difficult circumstances.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists build a nuclear clock that could make atomic clocks obsolete
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Scientists in Vienna have achieved a major breakthrough in timekeeping by creating the world’s first self-stabilizing nuclear clock, a technology that could eventually surpass even the most precise atomic clocks. Instead of relying on electrons in atoms, the clock uses the tiny nuclei of thorium atoms, which are far less sensitive to outside disturbances.

items.title: [Fast Company] South Korea’s bank hacks offer a warning about AI-powered cyberattacks
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Some of South Korea’s biggest banks have been hacked with the assistance of an artificial intelligence agent, opening up a new front in the AI and cybersecurity worlds.

Officials say at least seven financial firms were included in the attack, which saw personal information for 68,000 people stolen, including annual income and loan limits. This marks one of the first times AI tools have been used to disrupt global financial stalwarts.

It’s notable, since banks and other financial institutions typically have a higher level of security than other businesses or even some government agencies. Officials say they haven’t identified the people responsible for the attacks, which originated from over two dozen IP addresses spread out over several countries, including the U.S. and Japan. (Hackers frequently spoof their IP address to remain anonymous.)

South Korean officials are urging banks to boost their defenses. And the intrusions could serve as a warning shot for banks in the United States and other countries as well.

“AI gives attackers more opportunities to exploit gaps before defenders respond,” Yagub Rahimov, CEO of Polygraf AI, tells Fast Company. “My advice to bank leadership is to take a step back and invest in threat mapping. Trace the actual paths to sensitive data through employee activities, vendor connections, applications, APIs [application programming interfaces], and human and machine identities. They need to identify the systems that are reachable.”

The hackers apparently used Artex AI, an open-source agent developed in China, which ironically was designed as a cybersecurity tool that helped users find vulnerabilities in their networks. Artex has since updated its user guidelines to say the tool should not be used for malicious reasons.

AI-assisted hacking on the rise

While the attacks on the South Korean banks represent a new level, there has been a consistent uptick in AI-assisted hacking for some time now. A July report from the SANS Institute found that 78% of organizations saw either a confirmed or suspected AI-enabled attack in the past year.

The method of those attacks was evenly spread, though. Occurrences of phishing, deepfakes, and vulnerability exploitation were all virtually the same.

“AI tools are maturing, and so are the criminals using them—they moved from scaling phishing campaigns to autonomously probing defenses, chaining exploits, and adapting mid-attack,” Vakaris Noreika, cybersecurity expert at NordLayer Intelligence by NordStellar, tells Fast Company. “Going forward, we should expect attacks to grow in both scale and sophistication, which means defenses must keep pace with an AI-enabled threat landscape.”

The SANS Institute study showed a disparity between concern over possible AI-enhanced hacks and actual preparedness. Virtually every respondent—some 95%—said they believe threat actors are using AI today to enhance their attacks, with 58% saying they believe the use of AI is significant. Yet only 16% say they have shifted their priority to defend against such attacks.

Corrupting a tool

While Artex was designed to help protect users, the hackers’ use of this agent shows the range of possible threats that exist.

“The same capability that helps a security team investigate a weakness is also being used by an attacker to identify gaps for malicious purposes,” Rahimov says. “AI can connect tasks that previously required more manual work, making repeated attacks more economical—but even this can be turned around. Businesses should prepare for that capability to spread across tools and operators.”

Noreika warns that it’s not just smaller AI agent tools that can be corrupted, either. Most open-source AI models from a major lab possess the same advanced capabilities to hide malicious activity as security testing. That should put CEOs of banks and any other business on alert.

“The best way for companies to protect themselves is to adopt a hacker’s mindset—leveraging the very same AI tools to evaluate, stress-test, and strengthen their own security defenses,” Noreika says.

🏔️ ✏️

Appliance repairer Jacob D'Hollander qualifies for repair information under EU Ecodesign rules. Eight months of requests later, only one brand group has delivered.
